Threat.value: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

vignette:
Liam was twenty years old when he watched his older brother Marcus die. It happened in the parking lot of a gas station just off the interstate-a stupid argument over a parking space that spiralled into something none of them could have predicted. The other man pulled a knife. Liam saw the blade flash once, then disappear into Marcus's chest. What stayed with him, what he could still see in photographic stillness whenever he closed his eyes, was the way Marcus's hand had flown up to the wound, fingers splayed, blood welling between them. That hand. The fingers. The blood on the knuckles. He could not describe the event in words-every time he tried, the sentences scattered, and all he had were those frozen images, one after another like slides in a tray. And the smell: metallic, thick, the coppery scent of blood mixed with hot asphalt. It came back to him at odd moments-while cooking ground beef, while walking past a construction site, while his wife Sophie was on her period. He would gag and his heart would hammer and he would be back in that parking lot, the fluorescent lights buzzing overhead, the sound of his own voice screaming for someone to call 911.

In the months after, Liam stopped watching television altogether. He used to love crime dramas, but now even a trailer for a hospital show made his palms slick. Sophie would turn on a comedy, and he'd sit beside her on the couch, but his gaze would drift to the window, scanning the street for anyone who moved too quickly, too deliberately. A neighbour bending to pick up a newspaper made him flinch. A jogger rounding the corner made him hold his breath. He could not be alone in the apartment. If Sophie worked a late shift, he would walk to the all-night diner three blocks away and sit there nursing a coffee until she came home, because the silence of the empty rooms pressed against his ears and his mind threw up images of Marcus's hand, over and over, until he felt he was back in the parking lot, watching it happen again in real time. He began waking at 3 a.m., drenched in sweat, the smell of blood so vivid he had to check his own hands. Sleep became a battleground. He lay beside Sophie, listening to her breathe, terrified of what awaited him when his eyes closed.

He had no job now. Before the incident, he had been a mechanic at a local garage-good with his hands, proud of his work. But after, he could not bear the sight of grease under his nails. It reminded him of something, though he could not name it. He quit without explanation. His boss called twice; Liam did not call back. He had come to believe that his body had betrayed him. It kept reacting as if the danger were still there-heart racing, muscles taut, hands trembling-even when he was safe in his own living room. That meant he could not trust himself. He could not rely on his own judgment, his own reactions. The things that had once defined him-fixing engines, being the dependable younger brother, showing up for his family-felt like costumes he had shed and could not put back on. He had become someone who hurt himself. When the overwhelm grew too sharp, when the flashbacks pinned him in place and the smell filled his nostrils, he would lock himself in the bathroom and dig his fingernails into his forearm, or press a lit match against his thigh, just to feel something other than the terror. The physical pain gave him a moment of release, a clean sensation that cut through the chaos, and that was worth the bruises and burns Sophie would find later.

His marriage was straining under the weight of it. Sophie was patient, but she was also only twenty, and she did not understand why a comment about her own mother-a harmless remark about visiting for Thanksgiving-could send Liam into a cold silence for hours. He could not explain it. The word "family" landed in his chest like a stone. He avoided conversations about brothers, about holidays, about anything that touched the shape of what he had lost. He had stopped visiting his parents. His mother called and he let it go to voicemail.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a night when Sophie found him on the bathroom floor, a small kitchen knife in his hand, his wrist already bleeding. She did not scream. She knelt beside him, took the knife, and said, "I can't do this alone. We need help." He agreed because he could see that he was drowning her, too, and because he could not shake the terror that the next time he closed his eyes he would not be able to wake up. He was afraid of what he might do, but he was also afraid of never escaping the parking lot. He sat in the intake office with his hands clasped between his knees, unable to look the therapist in the eye, and said only, "I don't know how to make it stop. I don't even know how to tell you what happened."
